question: What is the purpose of @BeforeEach and @AfterEach in JUnit 5?
title: @BeforeEach @AfterEach JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **@BeforeEach runs a setup method before every single test.** @AfterEach runs a cleanup method after every test. They ensure each test starts with a fresh, known state — preventing tests from accidentally sharing state and causing flaky failures.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of test isolation and setup/teardown lifecycle
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a single shared instance across all tests causing tests to affect each other
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why fresh instances are critical for test independence and connect to the FIRST principles

sections.title: Fresh State for Every Test
sections.content: **@BeforeEach** typically instantiates the class under test and any fakes: `@BeforeEach void setUp() { service = new OrderService(mockRepo); }`. **@AfterEach** closes resources opened during the test: connections, streams. Without @BeforeEach, one test's side effects bleed into the next — classic cause of tests that pass individually but fail in suite.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- @BeforeEach: runs before each @Test — create fresh objects
- @AfterEach: runs after each @Test — release resources
- Execution order per test: @BeforeAll → @BeforeEach → @Test → @AfterEach → @AfterAll
- JUnit 5 creates a new test class instance per test (default)
- Multiple @BeforeEach allowed — order not guaranteed
- @BeforeAll/@AfterAll: static, runs once per class
- Use @BeforeEach over constructors for test setup

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @BeforeEach runs a method before every individual test method in the class. I use it to create a fresh instance of the class under test and initialize any mocks or test data. This ensures each test starts from a known, clean state. @AfterEach runs after each test — I use it to release resources like closing streams or verifying no unexpected Mockito interactions. Without @BeforeEach, if one test modifies state, it can affect subsequent tests, causing failures that only appear when tests run together — the worst kind of bug to debug.

groups.heading: @BeforeEach
groups.text: Runs a setup method before every individual @Test method. Use it to create a fresh instance of the class under test, initialize mocks, and reset any shared data. This ensures each test starts from a known, clean state.

groups.heading: @AfterEach
groups.text: Runs a cleanup method after every individual @Test method. Use it to release resources like file handles or streams. Even if the test throws, @AfterEach still runs — it's like a finally block.

values: Close resources and verify no surprises
Expensive shared setup like starting a DB

items: Use @BeforeEach whenever you'd otherwise duplicate setup code across multiple test methods
Use @AfterEach whenever a resource opened in a test (or @BeforeEach) must be explicitly closed

beats.text: In an OrderService test, @BeforeEach creates a fresh OrderService with a fresh mock repository before each test. Without it, if one test modifies the service's internal state, the next test inherits that mutation — a classic cause of tests that pass individually but fail in a suite.

speakable_v2.cap: Fresh state per test is the #1 rule for reliable tests — @BeforeEach is how you enforce it.

question: What does @DisplayName do in JUnit 5 and why should you use it?
title: @DisplayName JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **@DisplayName** provides a human-readable name for a test class or method that appears in test reports and IDE output. It lets you write descriptive sentences like 'should return zero tax when salary is below threshold' instead of method names like `testTaxCalcBelowThreshold`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of JUnit 5 improvements over JUnit 4
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing cryptic test method names like test1, test2 — which is useless in failure reports
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a realistic @DisplayName example and explain how it makes CI reports readable for non-developers

sections.title: Readable Names in Test Reports
sections.content: Test method names must follow Java naming rules (no spaces, no special chars). @DisplayName decouples the method name from the report name. `@Test @DisplayName("should throw IllegalArgumentException when age is negative") void test_age_validation_negative()`. In JUnit reports, CI dashboards, and IDE test trees, the @DisplayName string is shown — making it immediately clear what failed.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Applies to: @Test methods and test classes
- Value: plain English sentence describing the scenario
- Shows in: IDE test tree, Maven Surefire reports, CI dashboards
- Combine with @Nested for organized, readable test documentation
- Emojis allowed: @DisplayName("✅ should save customer when valid")
- Supports Unicode for international teams
- Alternative: method naming convention _when_then replaces DisplayName for simple cases

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @DisplayName in JUnit 5 provides a human-readable description for a test that appears in IDE output and CI reports instead of the method name. Java method names can't have spaces or special characters, so without @DisplayName you end up with names like testCalculateTaxBelowThreshold which is readable but less natural. With @DisplayName I can write 'should return 0 percent tax when salary is below minimum threshold' — this is self-documenting and non-developers like product managers can read test reports and understand what's covered.

question: What is @Disabled in JUnit 5 and when should you use it?
title: @Disabled JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **@Disabled** skips a test method or class, marking it as ignored in test reports. Use it when a test is known to fail due to a bug being tracked, when a feature is not yet implemented, or temporarily during development — always with a reason string explaining why.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical testing knowledge — the right way to skip tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Commenting out tests instead of using @Disabled — commented tests disappear from reports
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that @Disabled tests show up as 'skipped' in reports, which is visible and trackable, unlike commented tests

sections.title: Skip Visibly, Not Silently
sections.content: `@Disabled("Bug #1234 - fix in Sprint 15")` on a test method or class. The test appears as **skipped (not failed, not absent)** in reports — keeping visibility. **When to use**: (1) known failing test linked to a tracked bug, (2) feature not yet implemented, (3) flaky test under investigation. **When NOT to use**: to permanently hide failing tests — that masks quality. Always include a reason string.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- @Disabled on method: skips that test
- @Disabled on class: skips all tests in the class
- Always add reason: @Disabled("reason why")
- Shows as 'skipped' in reports — visible and trackable
- Don't comment out tests — they become invisible
- JUnit 4 equivalent: @Ignore
- @DisabledOnOs, @DisabledIf: conditional disabling based on conditions
- Tech debt: track all @Disabled tests and resolve them

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @Disabled skips a test and marks it as skipped in the test report. I use it when a test is failing due to a known bug that's tracked in the backlog — I annotate it with the bug ID so it's linked. The important thing is to always include a reason string explaining why it's disabled. The reason to prefer @Disabled over commenting out the test is visibility: skipped tests show up in CI reports as yellow, reminding the team they exist and need attention. Commented tests disappear completely. I treat accumulated @Disabled tests as technical debt that should be resolved.

beats.text: @Disabled marks a test method or class as skipped. The test doesn't run, but it appears as 'skipped' (yellow) in test reports rather than disappearing entirely. You can provide a reason string: @Disabled("Bug #1234 — fix expected in Sprint 15").

Sometimes a test fails because of a known tracked bug, an unimplemented feature, or a flaky behavior under investigation. Commenting out the test silently removes it from reports. @Disabled keeps it visible so the team knows it's there and can act on it.

items: On a method: skips only that test
On a class: skips every test in the class
Always include a reason string — @Disabled('reason') documents why it's off

CI shows it as skipped with the reason visible. candidates miss: @DisabledOnOs and @DisabledIf exist for conditional disabling based on environment or system properties — handy for tests that only apply on Linux or need a specific config flag.

question: What is @ExtendWith in JUnit 5 and when do you use it?
title: @ExtendWith JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **@ExtendWith** registers an extension that adds behavior to the test lifecycle — like integrating Mockito or Spring. `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` enables `@Mock` and `@InjectMocks` annotations automatically. It replaces JUnit 4's @RunWith.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know how to integrate Mockito or Spring with JUnit 5
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) in @BeforeEach instead of the cleaner @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @ExtendWith replaced @RunWith from JUnit 4, and that @SpringBootTest implicitly includes @ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)

sections.title: Extension Model for Integration
sections.content: JUnit 5's extension model is the hook for frameworks to inject behavior. `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`: processes `@Mock`, `@Spy`, `@InjectMocks` annotations — no manual `MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this)` needed. `@ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)`: integrates Spring context — but in Spring Boot projects, `@SpringBootTest` includes this automatically. Multiple extensions: `@ExtendWith({MockitoExtension.class, AnotherExtension.class})`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- JUnit 4: @RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class)
- JUnit 5: @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
- Enables: @Mock, @Spy, @InjectMocks, @Captor
- Spring Boot: @SpringBootTest includes SpringExtension automatically
- Multiple extensions allowed
- Can be placed on class or method
- Common extensions: MockitoExtension, SpringExtension, TemporaryDirectory
- Custom extension: implement BeforeEachCallback, AfterEachCallback etc.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @ExtendWith is JUnit 5's way of plugging in third-party frameworks. The most common one I use is MockitoExtension — adding @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to my test class tells JUnit to process @Mock, @Spy, and @InjectMocks annotations automatically before each test. Without it I'd have to call MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) in @BeforeEach manually. It replaces JUnit 4's @RunWith annotation. For Spring Boot integration tests, @SpringBootTest already includes SpringExtension so I don't need to add it separately.

speakable_v2.hook: @ExtendWith is JUnit 5's plug-in slot — that's where Mockito, Spring, and any other framework hooks into your test lifecycle.

beats.text: @ExtendWith registers an extension on a test class. Extensions can hook into any phase of the test lifecycle — before setup, after teardown, parameter injection, and more. It's JUnit 5's replacement for JUnit 4's @RunWith.

JUnit 5 was designed to be framework-agnostic. Instead of baking in Mockito or Spring support, it exposes an extension API. Mockito and Spring each provide their own extension, and you opt in with @ExtendWith.

items: @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class): processes @Mock, @Spy, @InjectMocks, @Captor automatically before each test
@ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class): integrates the Spring context — but @SpringBootTest includes this implicitly
Multiple extensions are allowed: @ExtendWith({MockitoExtension.class, AnotherExtension.class})

beats.text: Without @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) you'd have to call MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) manually in every @BeforeEach. Adding the annotation makes @Mock fields work automatically. production trap: forgetting @ExtendWith and then wondering why @Mock fields are null — the extension is required to initialize them.

items: Using @RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class) in a JUnit 5 project — @RunWith is JUnit 4 only; use @ExtendWith instead
Adding @ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class) when @SpringBootTest is already on the class — it's redundant, @SpringBootTest includes it

speakable_v2.cap: @ExtendWith is the bridge between JUnit 5 and every framework you want to use in tests — it's the first annotation to reach for when setting up Mockito.

question: What is @Nested in JUnit 5 and how does it improve test organization?
title: @Nested Tests JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **@Nested** allows inner test classes that group related tests together, creating a hierarchy. Outer class can contain @BeforeEach that applies to nested tests. It produces a readable tree structure in IDEs and CI reports showing test organization by scenario or method.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Having a flat list of 30 test methods in one class — @Nested provides structure without separate test files
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how @Nested + @DisplayName creates a test tree that reads like a specification

sections.title: Hierarchical Test Organization
sections.content: Inner classes annotated with @Nested group related scenarios. Example: outer class `OrderServiceTest`, nested class `@Nested @DisplayName("when order is empty")` with tests for that scenario, and `@Nested @DisplayName("when order has items")` with other tests. **@BeforeEach** in the outer class runs for all tests including nested ones. IDE shows a tree: OrderServiceTest > when order is empty > should throw, should return zero.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- @Nested: inner class that is a test container
- Creates hierarchical tree in reports
- Outer @BeforeEach applies to nested tests too
- Inner @BeforeEach only applies to that nested class's tests
- Combine with @DisplayName for specification-like structure
- Non-static inner class (unlike @BeforeAll which must be static)
- Replaces long flat list of test methods in one class
- Unlimited nesting depth (but 2-3 levels is practical)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @Nested lets me create inner test classes that group related test scenarios together. For example, for an OrderService I might have nested classes for 'when the cart is empty', 'when the cart has valid items', and 'when payment fails'. Each nested class has its own @BeforeEach for scenario-specific setup, but the outer class @BeforeEach also runs for all nested tests. The result is a tree structure in IDE and CI reports that reads like a specification — it's much easier to navigate than a flat list of 30 test methods. Combined with @DisplayName, the output reads almost like executable documentation.
